You can survive three minutes of severe bleeding, without breathable air (unconsciousness generally occurs), or in icy water.

You can survive three hours in a harsh environment (extreme heat or cold).

You can survive three days without drinkable water.

You can survive three weeks without edible food.

These conditions are assuming that the one(s) above it are met. For example, if you have a large quantity of food and water yet are exposed to the environment, then the harsh conditions rule applies. These rules are also useful in determining the order of priority when in a situation.

I just read through this thread and a major oversight is emergency communications (AKA EMCOM). in the event of a catastrophic situation where infrastructure can become crippled, how to you keep in touch with loved ones and the outside world?

  1. Make sure you can still receive information from the outside world. For better or worse, the Red Cross sells hand-crank, solar-charging radio, "Emergency Radios" with Weather Alerts and Smart Phone Chargers. There are quite a few options out there for this type of device but remember ""knowing is half the battle"" and when SHTF, you cannot have enough information.

  2. for family voice coms when in relative close proximity, consider the Family Radio Service ("FRS") or Multi-Use Radio Service ("MURS") walkie talkies or even a CB radio. None of these options requires special licensing. (there is also GMRS radios but that does require a license)

  3. for additional capability, like GPS and short range texting, there are off-grid options like the "GoTenna", the "Beartooth", and the "Sonnet"; to name a few. These types of devices are fairly new so the tech is not that mature. Also, each brand of these devices have various capabilities so do your homework. At the very least, if enough people utilize a MESH style system, then your communication range can extend indefinitely (and all without infrastructure).

  4. For wide range communications (including contacting emergency services, and listening to weather on NOAA frequencies) there is Amateur HAM radio service. Operating HAM radio equipment does require a licence but it is easy to get and costs $14ish for a 10 year license; Just ask Nellie Ohr (Call Sign "KM4UDZ"). The best resource for more information would be the "ARRL", which is the American Radio Relay League. Once licensed, a HAM operator can communicate on a wide range of devices and protocols. For example, simple $30 handheld on UHF frequencies can range a few miles. Setup a base station on VHF/UHF and now you can communicate much further (20+ miles based on conditions). And for a further reach there is HF radio which can literally span the globe and with no infrastructure but operating on HF does require a second license. Lastly, besides simple voice communications, Ham services have expanded to utilize many other modes of operations such as"APRS" for real time information sharing and tracking, or Packet Radio to send and receive data (including images).

Bottom line; Have a plan and communicate!
